title: Do the Work
author: Steven Pressfield
tagline: The 150-page kick in the pants that breaks through resistance and gets your project finished.
oneLiner: Resistance is the enemy of every creative act — and the cure is simple: start, continue, and finish. Do the work.
bigIdea: Pressfield's follow-up to The War of Art is a battle plan: every meaningful act — writing, starting a business, making art — faces Resistance, the force that keeps you from doing your work. The book is a short, punchy manual for the three phases of any project: starting (begin before you're ready), continuing (steady daily action beats bursts), and finishing (ship, don't polish forever). Resistance never goes away; you just outlast it.
quotes: The most important thing about art is to work. Nothing else matters except sitting down every day and trying.
The amateur believes he must first overcome all his fears before he can do his work. The professional knows that fear can never be overcome.

lessons.title: Resistance Is Universal
lessons.summary: Resistance is the force that acts against every act of creation — it shows up as procrastination, self-doubt, distraction, or the sudden urge to clean your desk. It's strongest when the work matters most. Knowing this makes you calm: the resistance you feel is proof you're on the right track.
lessons.example: The day you sit down to write your book is the day your house suddenly needs organizing. That's not coincidence — that's resistance, and it appears precisely because the work matters.
lessons.action: Next time you feel a sudden urge to avoid your project, say out loud: 'That's resistance.' Then stay at your desk.

lessons.title: Start Before You're Ready
lessons.summary: The biggest mistake amateurs make is waiting to feel ready. You will never feel ready — the work reveals itself only through the doing. Begin with what you have, where you are, even if it's terrible. Starting is a decision, not a feeling.
lessons.example: Pressfield wrote the first draft of his breakthrough novel badly and slowly — but he started it long before he felt like a 'real writer'. The book taught him what it needed to be. Pressfield's own story: he wrote the novel that broke his writer's block at dawn, before his day job, for two years — not because he was inspired, but because the professional shows up whether the muse visits or not. The work appeared only after the routine appeared.
lessons.action: Take the next step on your project right now — even a bad one. Readiness is a myth; motion is real.

lessons.title: The Professional Shows Up Daily
lessons.summary: Amateurs wait for inspiration; professionals have a schedule. The professional treats creative work like a job: same time, same place, every day, no matter the mood. This daily practice is what separates the finished novel from the good intentions.
lessons.example: Pressfield's rule: work every day, even when it's garbage. The garbage days are the price of the good days — and you can't have one without the other. His rule: 'finish, don't polish' — the first draft exists to be finished, and editing can only happen once there's something to edit. Amateurs polish page one forever; professionals finish the manuscript and then make it good.
lessons.action: Set a fixed daily work time for your project — 30 minutes minimum. Guard it like a medical appointment.

lessons.title: Finish, Don't Polish Forever
lessons.summary: Finishing is a separate skill from starting. Perfectionism is resistance in disguise — endless revision is just a socially acceptable way to avoid shipping. The professional finishes: declares the work done, sends it out, and starts the next thing.
lessons.example: Pressfield notes that many writers have 90% of a novel forever — the last 10% is where resistance fights hardest. The ones who finish are the ones who accept 'good enough' and let it go.
lessons.action: Pick the next milestone of your project and declare it finished by a date. When it hits 'good enough', ship it.

lessons.title: Act As If
lessons.summary: You become a professional by acting like one — before you feel like one. Act as if your work is serious, as if you have all the time in the world, as if nothing can stop you. The identity follows the behavior. In daily life, act As If rewards the patient and punishes the impatient — the difference is rarely talent and almost always consistency.
lessons.example: Pressfield's advice to struggling artists: dress like a professional, keep professional hours, treat your craft with professional respect — and the inner amateur starts to disappear. He quotes the painter who said 'inspiration is for amateurs — the rest of us just show up and work'. The muse rewards motion: every artist he profiles has a routine, and the routine is the real muse.
lessons.action: For one week, act as if your creative work is your real job: schedule it first, protect it, and refer to yourself as a professional.

lessons.title: The Muse Rewards Motion
lessons.summary: Inspiration doesn't arrive before work; it arrives during it. The muse shows up for the person already at the desk. The first hour is always the hardest — push through it and the work starts to carry you. In daily life, muse Rewards Motion rewards the patient and punishes the impatient — the difference is rarely talent and almost always consistency.
lessons.example: Pressfield describes how ideas that seem to 'come from nowhere' almost always surface in the middle of a work session — not while waiting. Motion attracts the muse. Pressfield describes writing a page a day during a family crisis — the smallest possible motion — and finding that the tiny daily act kept the work alive when a grand gesture would have collapsed. The muse shows up for the habit, not the heroics.
lessons.action: Commit to 25 minutes of your project right now. Don't stop to judge — just keep moving until the timer ends.

actionPlan: Name your resistance when it appears — don't fight it, outlast it.
Start your project today, ready or not.
Set a fixed daily work slot and protect it.
Declare your next milestone finished — and ship it.
Act as if: professional hours, professional respect, professional identity.
caveat: Pressfield's 'do the work, ship the work' is the creative professional's bible — and Shyp is the warning that shipping is not enough: the startup shipped relentlessly — millions in funding, beautiful product, perfect execution, growth every quarter — and still died when the economics of each shipment never worked. Pressfield's book is about overcoming resistance; Shyp's team overcame resistance beautifully and shipped themselves into a shutdown. The caveat for creatives-turned-founders: shipping the work and shipping a business are different verbs. Do the work — and also do the math. The work that doesn't pay rent is still art; it's just not a business yet.
